extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent classifiers and patent searchers (and patent attorneys preparing/classifying documents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for classifying patent documents into the International Patent Classification (IPC): how to interpret titles, definitions, groups and subgroups, how to treat invention vs additional information, chemical matter, combinations, details, and scope rules to determine appropriate classification places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — structured format and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions are prepared following a structured format; the most important part is the definition statement giving a more detailed explanation of the scope of the classification place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition statements use relevant words and phrases (often alternative to title wording) that appear in patent documents classified there. Definitions may include limiting and informative references, interpretation of special classifying rules affecting the place, and definitions of terms used in the place. Definitions are provided only for a limited number of subclasses and groups and will be elaborated progressively where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑limiting references in Definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting references indicating the location of subject matter of interest for searching are introduced into Definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These references do not limit the scope of the classification places with which they are associated; they are intended only to facilitate the patent search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of chemical formulae and graphic illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical structural formulae and other explanatory graphic illustrations can be introduced in the Classification scheme and in Definitions to provide visual representation and facilitate interpretation of scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some formulae are included in the scheme when necessary for defining or interpreting scope (example: main group C07D 499/00). Many additional formulae and graphic illustrations are presented in Definitions generally as examples; formulae are accessible via hyperlinks in relevant entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'covered' / 'provided for'
rubrics_metrics.description: When subject matter is stated to be 'covered' by/in a classification place, it means the subject matter has characteristics enabling it to be classified in that place. 'Provided for' has the same meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited (e.g., group A41F 18/00; B60Q 11/00) illustrate that wording in titles implying coverage indicates place is appropriate for such subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressions indicating residual subject matter ('not otherwise provided for')
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression 'not otherwise provided for' (or similar) in a group title means 'not provided for in any other group in the same subclass or in any other subclass'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups worded '... not provided for in groups ...' cover subject matter not provided for in stated groups. 'Other...' covers subject matter not provided for in related groups at same hierarchical level. Residual main groups usually occur at end of subclasses; however, use in a main group title does not expand scope of the subclass (see paragraph 55).

rubrics_metrics.name: Groups indicating combination subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Main groups worded '... covered by more than one of main groups ...' provide for subject matter consisting of a combination of characteristics not covered as a whole by a single specified group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups worded '... not covered by any single one of main groups ...' may provide both for combinations of characteristics and for subject matter not covered by any of the groups in the specified range (see example C05B 21/00).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and use of 'i.e.'
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression 'i.e.' has the sense of 'equals' and the two phrases joined by 'i.e.' are to be considered equivalent; one phrase defines the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Combines, i.e. harvesters or mowers combined with threshing devices' — the phrase after i.e. is a definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and use of 'e.g.'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'e.g.' does not limit the meaning of the preceding phrase; it provides an example or examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses: (a) typical illustration of subject matter; (b) to draw attention that what follows is definitely included even if not obvious; (c) to indicate matter covered by a group for which no dependent subgroup has been provided. Examples provided (A42C 5/00; B62B 7/00; G02B 6/122 etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical connectors: 'A and B', 'A or B', 'Either A or B, but not Both'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A and B' requires presence of both A and B in same example/embodiment; 'A or B' implies presence of A or B or both; 'either A or B, but not both' implies presence of A or B but not both in same example/embodiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret titles and subgroup headings using these logical meanings when determining essential characteristics for classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'in general', 'per se', 'specially adapted for'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In general' indicates characteristics considered disregarding any specific application; 'per se' concerns only an item itself as opposed to a combination; 'specially adapted for' indicates items modified or particularly constructed for a given use or purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Metallic powders per se' (B22F 1/00); 'Content per se' (H04N 21/80); 'FURNITURE SPECIALLY ADAPTED FOR CHILDREN' (A47D). Use these senses to choose function-oriented vs application-oriented places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'or the like'
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression 'or the like' emphasises that the classification place is not limited to the specific subject matter mentioned but also covers similar matter with essentially the same characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Non-abrasive sharpening devices for scythes, sickles, or the like' (A01D 3/00).

rubrics_metrics.name: Glossary: two‑part structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-part Glossary is included: first part for classification terms/expressions relating to principles and rules; second part for technical terms used in the Classification itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use glossary entries to clarify meaning of classification vocabulary and technical terms used throughout the Guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of a place must be interpreted within superior places
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of any classification place must always be interpreted within the scope of all its hierarchically superior places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles of sections/subsections/classes are broadly indicative only; subclass titles (with references/definitions/notes) define scope more precisely; main group and subgroup titles (with references/definitions/notes) define scope precisely. Always consider hierarchy and any references/notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances where a place covers more than its explicit scope (68bis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain circumstances, a place can cover more than its explicitly stated scope: (a) details/components specially adapted for the explicitly stated subject and not provided elsewhere; (b) combinations of the explicitly stated subject with other subject matter; (c) subject matter of a category not covered by the place and not covered elsewhere, but related to the explicitly stated subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include coverage of production when only product group exists. See paragraphs 92–98 for related rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of subclass scope (69)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of a subclass is defined together by: (a) the subclass title; (b) any limiting references following the subclass or class title; (c) any limiting references appearing in groups of the subclass that refer subject matter elsewhere; (d) any notes under the subclass title or its class/subsection/section title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting references can substantially alter apparent scope of subclass (example A47D excluding school benches/desks via A47B). The titles of subclasses may not embrace titles of all main groups under them; the scope should include all subject matter specifically stated in main group titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions elaborating subclass scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Where available, a Definition for a subclass provides a more detailed explanation of its scope and specifies exact boundaries of subject matter added to scope by main group titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult Definitions to resolve borderline scope questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main group scope rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of a main group is to be interpreted only within the scope of its subclass; the main group's scope is determined by its title as modified by any relevant references or notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a group 'bearings' in a subclass limited to a particular apparatus covers only features of bearings peculiar to that apparatus. Definitions may give more detail. Guidance headings are informative and do not as a rule define or modify scope (71bis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgroup scope and indentation interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of a subgroup is interpreted within the scope of its subclass, main group and any subgroup under which it is indented; the subgroup's scope is determined by its title as modified by relevant references/notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indentation indicates hierarchical reading — subgroup titles are read within and extending their parent group's meaning (example B64C 5/00 series for stabilising surfaces). Use references following titles to locate subject matter elsewhere (e.g., 'air-cushion vehicles B60V').

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgroup coverage and essential characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A subgroup covers only a particular part of the subject matter covered by the group under which it is indented; the scope of any subgroup compared to its parent group is determined by presence of one or more essential characteristics specified in the subgroup title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two cases: (a) essential characteristics not expressed in parent group title (example H01F 5/00 → 5/02); (b) essential characteristics already expressed in parent group title (example A63C 5/00 → 5/03).

rubrics_metrics.name: File scope of groups (74bis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that belongs to a subgroup should not be classified in its parent group. The 'file scope' of a group is the subject matter that should actually be classified in the group itself (residual subject matter), distinct from the group's complete scope which includes subgroups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When new subgroups are created the complete scope of the parent group remains unchanged but file scope is reduced. For groups without subgroups the scope and file scope are identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose of Classification — unique retrievability
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of the Classification is to facilitate retrieval of technical subject matter; it is devised and must be used so that the same technical subject is classified in, and thus can be retrieved from, one and the same place within the Classification — the place most relevant to be searched for that subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection of classification symbols follows same rules for 'invention information' and 'additional information'. Classify where searchers would expect to find the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention information — definition and determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention information is technical information in the total disclosure of a patent document that represents an addition to the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is determined in the context of the state of the art, using guidance provided by the claims, with due regard to description and drawings. 'Addition to the state of the art' means all novel and unobvious subject matter specifically disclosed in a patent document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional information — definition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional information is non-trivial technical information which does not in itself represent an addition to the state of the art but might constitute useful information for the searcher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It complements invention information by identifying constituents of a composition, elements/components of a process or structure, uses or applications, etc. The rules for selecting classification symbols apply equally to additional information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of subject matter (process/product/apparatus/material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical subject matter may represent processes, products, apparatus or materials (or the way these are used or applied); interpret these terms in their widest sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples for each category provided. Apparatus can be regarded as a product; 'product' denotes result of a process regardless of subsequent function; 'apparatus' is associated with intended use. Consider category when selecting places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Places to classify technical subjects as a whole (83)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Classification is designed to ensure any technical subject with which an invention is essentially concerned can be classified, as far as possible, as a whole and not by separate classification of constituent parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, constituent parts may themselves be invention information if novel and unobvious — in which case both whole and parts should be classified (see paragraph 91).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function‑oriented, application‑oriented and residual places (85–86)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification provides places for: (a) a thing 'in general' (function-oriented), (b) a thing 'specially adapted for' a particular use (application-oriented), (c) the particular use or application (application-oriented), (d) incorporation of a thing into a larger system (application-oriented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: F16K (function-oriented valves), A61F 2/24 (valve adapted for insertion into human heart), filters for particular purposes (application-oriented), B60G incorporation example. Places are not always exclusively function- or application-oriented; relative degrees may vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving function_vs_application classification ambiguity (90)
rubrics_metrics.description: When unclear whether to classify in a function-oriented or application-oriented place, follow rules: (a) if a particular application is mentioned but not specifically disclosed or fully identified, classify in function-oriented place if available; (b) if essential technical characteristics relate both to intrinsic nature and to particular use/adaptation/incorporation, classify in both places if available; (c) if (a) and (b) cannot be used, classify in both function-oriented and relevant application-oriented places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these steps to decide whether single or multiple classifications are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifying larger systems and novel parts (91)
rubrics_metrics.description: When classifying a larger system as a whole, attention should be given to parts or details whenever they are novel and unobvious; classification of both the system and these parts and details is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a document concerning incorporation of a leaf spring into vehicle suspension should be classified in place for the system (B60G) and, if leaf spring itself is novel/unobvious, also in place for the leaf spring (F16F).

rubrics_metrics.name: When a category is not explicitly provided by titles (92–99)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one category (e.g., product/apparatus/process) has no distinct place by title, use the most appropriate place existing for the other categories. Definitions and other means (references/notes) may indicate appropriateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific rules: chemical compounds per se → section C by chemical structure (93); mixtures/compositions → by composition if place exists, otherwise by use/application (94); preparation/treatment processes → place for process or, if none, place for compound (95); apparatus/process interplay rules (96); articles of manufacture → article place or function-oriented or field of use (97); multistep processes/industrial plants → classify as whole in combination place or else classify in place for product and separately classify elements (98); details/parts → classify in details places appropriate to their applicability, else classify in place for subject matter or according to all applicable kinds (99).

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic table default for chemical elements (92bis)
rubrics_metrics.description: In absence of contrary indication, the Periodic System of chemical elements referred to is the one with eight groups as represented in the table in the Guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, group C07F 3/00 referring to 'Groups 2 or 12' relates to columns IIa and IIb in that system; use this default unless otherwise specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of chemical compounds disclosed by general formulae (Steps 1–4)
rubrics_metrics.description: When general formulae (Markush-type) disclose large sets of related compounds, classification is restricted to compounds most useful for searches following a four-step procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 1: Classify all 'fully identified' compounds that are novel and unobvious if they are (i) specifically claimed as such or in a composition, (ii) products of a claimed process, or (iii) derivatives of these. 'Fully identified' means structure is exact name/formula or deducible from preparation from specified reactants (not more than one from a list) AND compound is characterised by a physical property or worked example with practical details. Compounds identified only by empirical formula are not 'fully identified'. Step 2: If no fully identified compounds disclosed (e.g., computer-generated, no experiments), classify only compounds with exact chemical name or developed formula, limited to a single or very small number of groups. Step 3: If only general Markush formula disclosed, classify in the most specific group(s) that cover all or most potential embodiments, limited to a single or very small number of groups. Step 4: In addition to obligatory classification, non-obligatory classification may be made when other compounds within scope of the general formula or compounds from computer-generated models are of interest.
